analysis.one_liner: Imposes disaster-preparedness fees, humane slaughter rules, and worker protections on large factory farms.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2023 with two Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets large industrial animal farming operations. Operators would have to register with USDA, submit disaster plans, pay annual fees, and bear the full cost of mass animal-killing events — including paying their workers severance and health coverage and compensating neighbors for health and property harm. It also bans the harshest mass-killing methods (like ventilation shutdown), ends programs that let slaughterhouses run at higher speeds with fewer federal inspectors, extends humane-slaughter law to poultry for the first time, and adds funding for workplace and food-safety inspectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry processing workers, who would get severance, two years of employer-paid health coverage, and whistleblower protections after disaster events; contract farmers, who would be compensated for lost revenue if a company cancels their contract after a disaster; people living near large feedlots, who could recover compensation for health impacts and property damage; small and higher-welfare farmers, who would gain inspection support and grants; and consumers and animals, through banned depopulation methods, humane-slaughter coverage for poultry, and more federal inspectors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Slaughterhouse workers, contract growers, rural neighbors

how_it_helps.text: Makes large industrial operators liable for all costs of disaster events and mass depopulations, including disposal, worker compensation, and harm to neighboring residents' health and property values.

Requires 12 weeks of severance for workers terminated after a disaster event, two years of employer-paid health coverage at silver-level benefits regardless of employment status, and lost-revenue payments to contract growers whose contracts are terminated.

Bans depopulation by ventilation shutdown, ventilation shutdown plus, sodium nitrite poisoning, and water-based foaming, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per animal and 10-year loss of federal contracts and inspection eligibility.

Terminates the programs that allow slaughter lines to run faster than standard limits or replace federal inspectors with company employees, and authorizes funding for additional OSHA and USDA food-safety inspectors.

Extends the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act to poultry, sets humane handling rules for livestock that can't walk, bans certain growth drugs tied to nonambulatory animals, and sets transport standards for trips longer than 8 hours.

Provides $750 million in grants to help poultry plants switch from live-shackle slaughter to controlled-atmosphere stunning, and a $50 million pilot program expanding inspection access for small processing facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Large industrial farm operators and big meatpackers and poultry processors, through annual fees, full liability for disaster costs, new labor mandates, the loss of faster slaughter-line and self-inspection programs, and humane-handling rules. A portion of the grant funding ($750 million plus inspection programs) would come from the Treasury. Some costs could surface as slightly higher meat prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large factory farms and meat processors

drawbacks.text: Annual fees of at least $1 per animal unit and full liability for disaster costs would raise operating expenses for large operators, costs that could partly reach consumers through higher meat prices.

The bill appropriates $750 million for the stunning transition grants and authorizes roughly $1.7 billion more over a decade for OSHA and food-safety inspectors, new federal spending paid by taxpayers.

Grant eligibility is limited to facilities with labor peace agreements with unions, and grantees are barred for 10 years from selling to or merging with any packer holding more than 10% market share — conditions that would exclude some otherwise willing plants.
Several of its biggest changes are delayed: poultry is added to the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act and the tightened 8-hour transport limit only take effect 10 years after enactment.

In a disaster, operators could face the choice between paying full depopulation, disposal, and compensation costs or holding animals past their slaughter dates, a compliance burden the bill acknowledges by requiring plans for alternative processing capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits fall on groups with little market power — low-wage slaughterhouse workers, contract farmers dependent on a handful of companies, and rural neighbors of feedlots — while its costs fall on some of the most concentrated businesses in the food system. The bill's own findings note operators saw 300% profit growth during the COVID-19 pandemic while more than 60 million poultry and 10 million swine were killed, often by methods the bill would ban. Its main design weaknesses are the 10-year phase-ins for poultry slaughter and transport rules and the heavy new spending authorizations; but because it never advanced, none of these trade-offs were ever tested in a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in February 2023, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Industrial Agriculture Accountability Act of 2023 in the Senate on February 2, 2023, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Brian Schatz.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which was its only action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill ended the Congress with two cosponsors, both Democrats, and was never voted on in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large industrial livestock operators and meat processors, who face none of the bill's fees, disaster liability, labor mandates, or end of faster slaughter-line and self-inspection programs. Workers, contract growers, and rural communities remain without the protections the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large industrial livestock and meat companies

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled its disaster-mitigation, labor, and humane-slaughter provisions.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsorships it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 2, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Industrial meat and poultry trade associations
against.role: Industry lobby for large meatpackers, poultry processors, and livestock producers
against.what_they_did: Groups representing large meat and poultry companies have consistently opposed mandatory spending, liability, and slaughter-speed restrictions of this kind; no committee action was ever scheduled on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no voting record exists; all three supporters were Democrats, and the bill never progressed far enough to attract or reveal Republican opposition.

industries.industry: Large industrial livestock and poultry operators
industries.note: The bill charges them annual fees, makes them liable for all disaster and depopulation costs including damages to neighbors, bans their cheapest mass-killing methods, and bars incarcerated labor. Their cost savings from weak disaster planning and harsh depopulation methods come directly at the expense of workers, animals, and rural communities.

It terminates the New Swine and New Poultry Inspection Systems that allow faster line speeds and company self-inspection, extends humane-slaughter law to poultry, and requires union labor peace agreements as a grant condition. Faster lines and reduced inspection lower their labor and oversight costs, which the bill's findings tie to unsafe conditions for workers.

industries.industry: Small, regional, and higher-welfare farmers and processors
industries.note: The bill funds a pilot program expanding inspection access for small processing facilities and grants to plants transitioning to controlled-atmosphere stunning, aiming to level a market the bill describes as highly monopolized by industrial operators.

The bill bans use of drugs like ractopamine, zilpaterol, and lubabegron for growth promotion or feed efficiency, eliminating a market for these products; the bill links them to livestock becoming unable to walk.
